passages.t: John the Baptist in the wilderness
passages.happening:
About thirty years pass between chapter 2 and chapter 3. Jesus has grown up in Nazareth. Now a new voice is heard. John the Baptist appears in the wilderness of Judea, the dry, empty country near the Jordan River, and his message is short: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (verse 2).

To repent means to turn around: to change your mind and your direction, to stop going away from God and come back. People pour out to John from Jerusalem, from all Judea and from the towns along the Jordan. They confess their sins out loud and he baptizes them in the river. To baptize means to dip or wash in water; here it is a sign that a person is turning from sin and getting ready for God.
passages.hearers:
Two things about John would make a Jewish hearer sit up.

His clothes. John wore camel's hair and a leather belt. That is how the Bible describes the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). And the last words of the Old Testament promise: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). John is dressed as that sign.

His food. Locusts and wild honey were food the law allowed (Leviticus 11:22) and that the wild land gave for nothing. John lived on what he did not have to buy.

The place mattered too. The wilderness was where Israel had been formed after leaving Egypt, and the Jordan was the river they crossed into the promised land. Going out to the wilderness and down into the river was like going back to the start of Israel's story to begin again.

Notice something Matthew does. John's first words are exactly the same as Jesus' first words later (4:17). John and Jesus preach one message.
passages.ot: Matthew quotes Isaiah 40:3, a voice calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord.’ In Isaiah these words open the great promise of comfort for Israel after exile: God himself is coming back to his people, and a road must be made ready for him. Matthew says John is that voice. That means the one coming after John is the Lord himself.
passages.asks: John's message was simple and costly: turn around. The people who came to him did not only feel sorry; they said their sins out loud. Is there something you have never named before God? What would turning around look like for you this week?

passages.t: A warning, and the one who is coming
passages.happening:
When John sees many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to be baptized, he turns on them: “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (verse 7). Show by your lives that you have turned, he says. Do not lean on being Abraham's children. God could make children for Abraham out of these stones.

The axe is already at the root of the trees, he warns. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and burned.

Then John points away from himself. I baptize with water, he says. But someone more powerful is coming after me, and I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. He has his winnowing fork in his hand. He will gather his wheat into the barn and burn up the chaff.
passages.hearers:
The Pharisees and Sadducees were two of the main groups in Jewish life. The Pharisees were teachers who worked hard to keep God's law in daily life, and they were popular with ordinary people. The Sadducees were mostly from the priestly families who ran the temple, and they did not believe in the resurrection of the dead or in angels (Acts 23:8). The two groups often disagreed. Here they come together, and John speaks to both the same way.

‘Brood of vipers’ means a nest of snakes. Snakes flee when a field is set on fire. John's picture is of snakes running from the flames, not people truly turning to God. Jesus will use the same words later (12:34; 23:33).

‘We have Abraham as our father’ was a real comfort. Being part of Abraham's family meant being part of God's people. John says that is not enough on its own. There may also be a play on words. In Hebrew, ‘stones’ is abanim and ‘children’ is banim. God can raise up banim from abanim.

Carrying a master's sandals was a servant's lowest job. John says he is not fit even for that.

Every farmer knew winnowing. After the harvest, the grain was beaten on an open threshing floor. Then the farmer tossed it into the air with a wooden fork. The wind blew away the light chaff, the husks, and the heavy grain fell back to be gathered. The chaff was swept up and burned. John says the coming one already has the fork in his hand. The sorting is about to begin.
passages.ot: John's fire comes from the prophets. Malachi had warned that the coming day would be “burning like a furnace,” and the proud would be stubble (Malachi 4:1). He had also asked, “But who can endure the day of His coming?” (Malachi 3:2). Baptism ‘with the Holy Spirit’ also had roots in the prophets: God had promised, “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28), and a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26). The fire both cleans and judges.
passages.hard: John's words are hard to hear. Is this the voice of love? John speaks this way because he thinks the danger is real and close. A warning shouted at someone walking toward a cliff is not unkind. Notice also whom he aims it at: not the crowds confessing their sins, but religious leaders who come without any sign of turning. Every reader who feels safe because of their religious family or background is meant to feel the axe at the root. Being born into a Christian family is as little protection as being born into Abraham's.
passages.asks: John asks for ‘fruit’: a changed life you can see. What would someone see in your life that shows you have turned toward God? And what do you lean on instead of turning, your family, your church, your past?

passages.happening:
Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. John tries to stop him: “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” (verse 14). Jesus answers, “Let it be so now.” And he adds, “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way” (verse 15). So John baptizes him.

As Jesus comes up out of the water, heaven opens. He sees the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him. And a voice from heaven says, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
John's baptism was for people turning from their sins. So why would Jesus come? John himself is shocked. Matthew is the only Gospel to tell us John's protest and Jesus' answer, perhaps because his readers asked the same question.

The open heavens would make a Jewish hearer remember Isaiah's prayer: “If only You would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). Many felt heaven had been closed and silent for a long time. Now it opens.

The dove is not explained, and readers have heard echoes in it. At creation the Spirit of God hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2), and after the flood a dove brought Noah the sign of a new world (Genesis 8:11). Either way, the Spirit rests on Jesus, as the prophets said God's Spirit would rest on his chosen one.

Notice that all three are present. The Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down, the Father speaks. Christians have long seen in this scene the God the church later confessed as Trinity: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
passages.ot: The Father's words join several passages. “You are My Son” is how God speaks to his anointed king in Psalm 2:7. ‘In whom I am well pleased’ echoes God's servant in Isaiah 42:1, “My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him.” And ‘beloved Son’ may recall Genesis 22:2, where God speaks of Isaac as Abraham's “only son Isaac, whom you love.” King, servant and beloved son: the voice names in advance the road Jesus will walk, from a king's authority to a servant's death.
passages.hard: Why was the sinless Jesus baptized? Christians have given several answers, and they fit together. Some stress obedience: righteousness in Matthew means doing God's will, and this was God's will for him, so Jesus does it fully. Some stress that Jesus stands with sinners: he steps into the water beside the people he came to save, taking their place long before the cross. Some stress fulfilment: Matthew uses ‘fulfil’ for the promises coming true, and Jesus is beginning the work God promised. What the passage does not mean is that Jesus had sins to confess. John himself says it is the other way round.
passages.asks: The Father calls Jesus ‘beloved’ and ‘well pleased’ before Jesus has preached a sermon or done a single miracle. Christians believe that those who belong to Jesus share in that love. Do you live as if God's love must be earned first? What would change if you began each day from being loved, not working toward it?
